The GitHub Docs concept page "Self-hosted runners" notes that self-hosted runners do not need a clean instance for every job. That also means nothing cleans up for you. An ephemeral runner is registered once and takes one job:

./config.sh --url ORG_URL --token TOKEN --ephemeral

Per "Self-hosted runners reference", the lifecycle is:

  1. Register with --ephemeral.
  2. GitHub assigns one job to that runner.
  3. After the job, the GitHub Actions service de-registers the runner.
  4. Your automation wipes the machine, or discards the VM or container, and registers a new runner with a new token.

GitHub recommends ephemeral runners for autoscaling and advises against autoscaling persistent runners, because in some cases a job can be sent to a persistent runner while it is shutting down. A clean environment per job also limits what one job leaves behind for the next. The same page asks you to forward ephemeral runner logs to external storage, since the machine and its logs are gone after the job.

Just-in-time (JIT) runners through the REST API

Instead of config.sh --ephemeral, you can create ephemeral, just-in-time runners with the REST API, described on "REST API endpoints for self-hosted runners". The generate-jitconfig endpoint returns an encoded configuration that you pass to the runner at start with ./run.sh --jitconfig. A JIT runner is single-use and skips the separate token and config step, which suits a script that boots a VM and starts one runner inside it.

Routing, queueing and runner updates

From "Self-hosted runners reference":

  • GitHub sends a job to an online, idle runner that matches its runs-on labels and groups. If that runner does not pick it up within 60 seconds, the job is re-queued.
  • If no matching runner is online, the job waits, and fails after 24 hours in the queue.
  • Runners update themselves by default, so every fresh VM or container image starts by updating. Register with --disableupdate and update the image on your own schedule.
  • With updates off, update within 63 days of a new runner version, or GitHub stops assigning jobs to that runner.

Ways to get a clean environment per job

The autoscaling routes below come from "Self-hosted runners reference", plus Potluck. All pair with ephemeral or JIT runners.

OptionWhat it does wellWhat it needs from you
Persistent runner (config.sh, run.sh)Simplest install, warm cachesManual cleanup; jobs share one disk
--ephemeral with your own scriptsOne job per registrationWipe and re-register logic, token fetching, log forwarding
JIT runner via REST APISingle-use, no separate token stepCode that calls the API and boots a fresh machine
Actions Runner Controller (ARC)GitHub's reference implementation, full lifecycleA Kubernetes cluster and people to run it
Runner Scale Set Client (actions/scaleset)Go module for VMs, containers and macOSYou write the provisioning
workflow_job webhookScaling built exactly as you wantYour own service; depends on timely webhook delivery
Potluck runner brokerFresh Tart VM on a Mac, or gVisor or Kata sandbox on Linux, on machines you ownEarly; run by hand so far, not yet daily in its makers' CI

Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without a Sengi account.

Self-hosted macOS runners with an ephemeral VM per job

ARC targets Kubernetes, which does not run macOS. On a Mac, the clean-per-job pattern is: boot a macOS VM from an image, start one ephemeral or JIT runner inside it, delete the VM after the job. Tart is a common way to run those VMs on Apple silicon. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so plan for two concurrent macOS jobs per Mac. Lending those VMs to your team is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice. See our Tart page and self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac.

Where Potluck fits

Potluck is free, open-source (Apache-2.0) software that runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on machines a team already owns, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. It drives Tart on an Apple silicon Mac and Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. It is not a sandbox runtime of its own, not a hosted cloud and not a cluster scheduler.

What works today: a real Actions job has been run through Potluck's runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine with gVisor. It is not yet in daily use in its makers' own CI. Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer; on Linux, hand-back to a returning owner works only as a time window today.

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including repository secrets, and the machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use it at your own risk. More on the GitHub Actions runner page and in pool spare Macs and Linux boxes.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that runs the pool (the first create prints a Tailscale login URL):

potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host

On the Mac mini or Linux box that will share:

potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'

potluck host checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a conformance check per size and joins only when a size passes. --share (default 0.5) sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, and potluck host stop stops sharing. potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. To contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

Questions people ask

How long is a self-hosted runner registration token valid?

One hour, according to the GitHub Docs page "Adding self-hosted runners". Automation that registers runners later should fetch a fresh token through the REST API.

What is the difference between --ephemeral and a JIT runner?

Both take one job and are then removed. --ephemeral is a config.sh flag used with a registration token; a JIT runner gets an encoded config from the REST API and starts with ./run.sh --jitconfig.

Can a macOS self-hosted runner run Docker container actions?

No. "Self-hosted runners reference" says Docker container actions and service containers need a Linux machine with Docker installed.

What happens if no self-hosted runner is online?

The job stays queued and fails after 24 hours, per "Self-hosted runners reference".

How many macOS VMs can I run per Mac for ephemeral runners?

Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. This is not legal advice.

Is Potluck ready to replace my CI runners?

Not yet. A real Actions job has run through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on Linux, but it is not in daily use in its makers' CI, and it is early software.

Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted runners, but it runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

entry.title: Give Coding Agents Their Own Mac: macOS VMs on a Mac mini (2026)
entry.summary: One Mac mini can give coding agents two macOS VMs at once. How Tart, UTM, Lima and Potluck compare for safe, disposable agent sandboxes on Apple silicon.
entry.content:
Short answer: one Apple silicon Mac mini can give coding agents two macOS VMs at a time, because Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own. Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac for the same reason. The usual way to do it is Tart: clone a fresh macOS VM for each task, run the agent in it headless, and delete the VM when the task ends. UTM suits people who want the VM in a window, and Lima is built around Linux guests. Potluck, an early, free and open-source (Apache-2.0) project, drives Tart on your Macs and Kata or gVisor on Linux, so an agent gets a fresh sandbox per task through a command line or an MCP server without you writing the VM lifecycle yourself.

The options compared

Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account.

OptionWhat it runs on a MacBest atDisposable per taskHow an agent gets inWork you do
TartmacOS and Linux VMs on Apple siliconHeadless, scripted macOS guests from registry imagesYes, if you clone and delete per taskYour own scripts around its exec commandWrite and maintain the lifecycle scripts
UTMmacOS, Linux and Windows guests, with a GUIInteractive use, trying an OS in a windowPossible, mostly by handYou shell into the guestMore manual steps for automation
LimaLinux VMs, often used for containersLinux dev environments on a MacYes, for Linux guestsShell or container toolsNot the tool for a macOS guest
Hosted Macs (cloud or hosted runners)Machines you rentNo hardware to look afterDepends on the providerProvider's API or runnerYou pay for rented time
PotluckTart guests on Macs, Kata or gVisor sandboxes on LinuxFresh sandboxes for agents and Actions jobs on machines you ownYes, each run in a fresh VM or sandboxpotluck sandbox commands or the MCP serverInstall, create a pool, host a machine

Why an agent needs its own Mac

A coding agent that builds a Mac app, clicks through its UI or installs tools wants the whole machine. On your desktop it competes with you for the keyboard, the pointer and the front window, and it can reach your files, your keychain and your shell history. A macOS VM fixes both: the agent gets a desktop of its own, and when the task ends you throw the VM away so the next task starts clean.

A developer blog post from November 2026, about running a Mac card game's UI tests in a VM, describes the pattern well: Xcode and the source stay on the host, the host builds a Debug app, the app is copied into a headless macOS guest, and the agent drives it there and reads back a screenshot and the accessibility tree. The host Mac stays usable the whole time.

The two-VM limit on a Mac mini

The number that shapes every plan is two. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac to match. A Mac mini therefore gives you at most two agent Macs at once. For more parallel macOS agents you need more Macs, and Linux sandboxes on other boxes can take the work that does not need macOS.

The licence also limits who uses those guests. Lending a macOS guest to your team or to invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

Doing it by hand with Tart

Tart, from Cirrus Labs, is the most direct route. You install it with Homebrew, use tart clone to pull a macOS image from a container registry into a named VM, start it headless with tart run, and send commands into the guest with tart exec. Use the prebuilt images that include Tart's guest agent, since exec needs it; the vanilla images lack it. The images are large, so check free disk space first, and pick the macOS version your app needs as its minimum.

To make the VM disposable, clone a fresh copy from the base image for each task and delete it afterwards. That loop is what you end up scripting: create, wait for the desktop, copy the build in, run, collect output, delete. It works well, and you own every line of it. For more on Tart, see our Tart page.

UTM and Lima: where they fit

UTM is a good app for running macOS, Linux and Windows guests in a window on Apple silicon. It is the friendlier choice when a person sits in front of the VM. For an agent that needs a fresh guest every few minutes, you do more by hand than with Tart.

Lima is a solid way to run Linux VMs on a Mac, often as the base for containers. If your agent only needs a Linux shell, a Lima VM on the Mac mini is a fine sandbox. For a macOS guest, people reach for Tart or UTM instead.

Making the VM safe, and what safe means

A fresh VM per task stops one task from leaving files or processes behind for the next. Beyond that:

  • Network. Decide what the guest can reach. With Potluck, potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On Potluck's OCI layer on Linux, the default is no network at all.
  • Secrets. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including any secret you pass in. Give an agent only the tokens the task needs.
  • The person at the Mac. On a desk Mac, Potluck ends a Mac sandbox when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. A Mac mini in a cupboard has nobody touching it, so it stays available.

Start with Potluck

Potluck is early. On macOS or Linux, with no Go needed:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that runs the pool (the first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL), create the pool and make a code for a machine to share:

potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host

Is Tart or UTM better for an AI agent sandbox?

Tart, for most agent setups, because it is built for headless, scripted guests and has a guest agent for running commands. UTM is better when a person wants to use the VM in a window.

Can I use Lima to give an agent a macOS VM?

Lima is built around Linux guests. Use it when a Linux shell is enough, and use Tart or UTM when the agent needs macOS.

Not from the machine running it: that machine can read everything in the VM, including secrets, and a pool's machine can read commands and output passing through it. Pass in only what the task needs and join only pools whose owner you trust.

No. Potluck is free, open source under Apache-2.0, and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account.

entry.title: Local Alternatives to Cloud AI Coding Sandboxes (November 2026)
entry.summary: Local, open-source alternatives to cloud AI coding sandboxes like E2B and Daytona, compared, plus pooling the Macs and Linux boxes your team owns.
entry.content:
Short answer: the local alternatives to cloud AI coding sandboxes such as E2B and Daytona are open-source tools that run the same kind of isolated box on hardware you control. The main ones are E2B's own open-source runtime, microsandbox, Hotcell, agent-sandbox for Kubernetes and agentbox, plus the runtimes underneath them: Firecracker, gVisor, Kata Containers, nsjail and bubblewrap. The software is free to use. You pay in hardware and in the hours it takes to run it. Potluck takes a different route: free, Apache-2.0 software that pools the Macs and Linux boxes a team already owns and gives each agent a fresh VM or sandbox on one of them, with GitHub Actions jobs served from the same pool. Potluck is early, and it is made by Sengi, a company that sells hosted GitHub Actions runners.

Local alternatives at a glance

OptionWhat it isIsolationRuns onWhere it needs more work
E2B open-source runtimeThe runtime behind E2B's managed serviceFirecracker microVMsCloud accounts you operateYou run the same distributed system E2B runs
microsandboxEmbeddable library, no long-running daemonlibkrun microVMsApple silicon Macs, Linux with KVM, WindowsYou wire it into your own agent code
HotcellSandbox layer with a key-swapping gateway on the hostDocker, Firecracker, Apple VirtualizationOne Mac, Linux box or VMSized to one machine; non-HTTP credentials still have to be injected
agent-sandboxKubernetes resource and controllergVisor or Kata via RuntimeClassAny Kubernetes clusterYou need to run a cluster
agentboxContainer wrapper for one developer's agentDocker plus an egress proxy and firewallYour own machineContainer boundary, one developer
Firecracker, gVisor, Kata, nsjail, bubblewrapBuilding blocksmicroVM, user-space kernel, VM-backed containers, Linux namespacesLinuxYou build lifecycle, networking and cleanup yourself
PotluckA pool of a team's own machines for agent sandboxes and Actions jobsTart on Apple silicon; Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on LinuxMacs and Linux boxes you own, joined over TailscaleEarly; Linux hand-back is only a time window today

Why teams move agent sandboxes off the cloud

Managed sandboxes are the least work. One API call and a box appears, and someone else patches the kernels. That is worth a lot, and for a team with no spare hardware it is often the right call.

The reasons people search for local alternatives are usually three:

  • Where the code runs. Some repositories cannot leave company machines because of a client contract or policy.
  • The meter. One agent session is cheap. Many agents running all day on per-second billing adds up, especially when Macs and Linux boxes sit idle on desks.
  • Control. You pick the image, the network rules and when a box dies.

Running locally does not make the model provider go away. Your prompts and code still go to whichever model the agent calls, unless you run the model yourself too.

The options, one by one

E2B's open-source runtime

The runtime behind E2B's managed service is open source. It runs Firecracker microVMs with snapshot, pause and resume, and can be deployed into cloud accounts you operate. It is the closest thing to self-hosted E2B, and the most operational work on this list.

microsandbox

microsandbox runs OCI images in microVMs built on libkrun, as a library with no server. It works on Apple silicon Macs, Linux with KVM and Windows, has SDKs for several languages, and supports secrets that never enter the VM. Good for builders who want sandboxing inside their own program.

Hotcell

Hotcell runs as many sandboxes as one machine can hold, using Docker, Firecracker on Linux with KVM, or Apple Virtualization on macOS. Its strength is credentials: each sandbox gets a short-lived token, and a gateway on the host swaps it for the real key. Its own documentation says credentials that do not travel in an HTTP header still have to be injected.

agent-sandbox for Kubernetes

If agents already run on Kubernetes, agent-sandbox adds a Sandbox resource with templates and warm pools. Isolation comes from the cluster's RuntimeClass, usually gVisor or Kata. It is a good fit for platform teams and a heavy one for a team without a cluster.

agentbox

agentbox wraps a coding agent in a Docker container with an egress proxy, and injects secrets through the proxy so the agent never sees them. Lightweight, and aimed at a single developer.

The building blocks

Firecracker gives a separate guest kernel through KVM. gVisor puts a user-space kernel between the container and the host. Kata gives VM-backed containers that keep OCI and Kubernetes interfaces. nsjail and bubblewrap confine a Linux process with namespaces, mounts and syscall filters. All are solid, and none is a finished agent product: you write the lifecycle, mounts, network policy and cleanup. Agent harnesses such as OpenHands sit on top and still need one of these as the boundary.

What about Daytona?

Daytona's README says core development moved to a private codebase and the public repository no longer gets updates. You can fork the last open release, but it is not a maintained local option.

A different approach: pool the machines you already own

Every tool above answers "how do I isolate code on this machine or cluster?" Potluck answers a different question: "we have spare Macs and Linux boxes on desks; how do we put them to work for agents and CI?"

Potluck is not a sandbox runtime of its own. It drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus. It is not a hosted cloud and not a scheduler for clusters. One machine runs a pool, teammates and invited friends join it, and some of them lend machines to it. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure.

What that changes for the reader:

  • The Mac on someone's desk is usable. A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer, and when an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
  • One pool, two jobs. The same pool serves coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. A real Actions job has been run through the runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in our own CI. potluck agent-runner runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.
  • Agents get tools directly. potluck --pool friends mcp is an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent. More in give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP.

What a local sandbox still has to get right

Local does not mean safe by default. With Potluck, potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet, and on the OCI layer the default is no network at all.

Be clear about trust. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Potluck does not swap API keys behind a gateway the way Hotcell, microsandbox or agentbox aim to. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use it at your own risk.

For Macs, Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.

How to choose

If you needStart with
Self-hosted E2B at cloud scaleE2B's open-source runtime
A microVM library inside your own programmicrosandbox
Real API keys never inside the sandbox, on one hostHotcell
Sandboxes as Kubernetes resourcesagent-sandbox
A quick container for one developer's agentagentbox
Full control of every layer on LinuxFirecracker, gVisor, Kata, nsjail or bubblewrap
Agent sandboxes and Actions jobs on the team's spare Macs and Linux boxesPotluck

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that will run the pool, create it. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL.

potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host

Ana runs potluck join '<code>' to use sandboxes. Carl runs potluck host '<code>' to share a machine. Before that, potluck doctor shows what the machine can share and potluck host --dry-run prints the plan. potluck host checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. --share sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared (default 0.5, per the Potluck docs). potluck host stop stops sharing.

Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac (see Tart), or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. Then try a sandbox:

potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>

For a longer walk-through, read run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines and pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents.

What makes Potluck different

  • It uses the machines you already own. Instead of renting sandboxes, agents run on the team's idle Macs and Linux boxes, each in a fresh VM or sandbox.
  • A Mac goes back to its owner the moment they touch the keyboard or pointer, so lending a desk machine does not mean giving it up.
  • One pool serves agents and CI. Coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs come from the same pool, though Actions is not yet in daily use in our own CI.
  • Teammates and invited friends can lend machines to the same pool, and agents reach it through sandbox tools over MCP.
  • It is free and open source (Apache-2.0) and runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues. The source is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.

Questions people ask

What is the best local alternative to E2B?

For E2B's own architecture on cloud accounts you run, use E2B's open-source runtime. For one machine with keys kept out of the sandbox, look at Hotcell or microsandbox. For a pool of the team's own Macs and Linux boxes, try Potluck.

Can I run AI coding sandboxes on a Mac?

Yes. microsandbox and Hotcell support Apple silicon, and Potluck runs macOS guests through Tart, capped at two per Mac to match Apple's licence.

Do local sandboxes keep my code private?

They keep execution on machines you control. Code and prompts still go to the model provider the agent calls, and with Potluck the machine running a VM can read everything inside it.

Does Potluck keep API keys out of the sandbox?

No, it does not claim to. The host machine can read secrets in a VM, so if key isolation is your main need, Hotcell, microsandbox or agentbox focus on it.

Is Daytona still open source?

Its last open release can still be forked, but its README says development moved to a private codebase and the public code gets no further updates.

Can Potluck run GitHub Actions jobs too?

A real Actions job has been run through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but not yet daily in our own CI. See GitHub Actions runner for the current state.

Is Potluck a hosted service?

No. It is free, open-source software you run yourself, and it needs no Sengi account.

entry.title: Open source sandbox for AI coding agents, self-hosted (2026): Claude Code sandboxing and your own hardware
entry.summary: What Claude Code's Bash sandbox isolates, what it leaves out, and open-source sandboxes for AI coding agents you can run on your own hardware in 2026.
entry.content:
Short answer: In November 2026 you have two layers to choose from. The first is the sandbox built into Claude Code. It is off by default; you turn it on with /sandbox. It confines only the shell commands Claude runs: writes are limited to the working directory, and network access goes through a proxy that checks each host against an allowlist. The second layer puts the whole agent, or the commands it runs, inside a container or VM. Open-source tools for that second layer include Anthropic's sandbox runtime, OpenSandbox (Apache-2.0, on Docker or Kubernetes) and Potluck (Apache-2.0, free, early). Potluck runs each sandbox in a fresh VM or sandbox on Macs and Linux boxes your team already owns. Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners; Potluck itself is a separate free project.

The options compared

OptionWhat it isolatesWhere it runsOpen sourceWhere it costs more or needs more work
Claude Code Bash sandboxShell commands and their child processesYour own machine: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2Built on Anthropic's open-source sandbox runtimeFile tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it; reads most of your disk by default
Anthropic sandbox runtime around the whole processThe Claude Code process itselfYour own machineYesYou write and maintain the filesystem and network policy
Dev container or local VMEverything inside the container or VMYour own machineDepends on the toolUses your laptop's cores and RAM; setup per project
OpenSandboxAgent commands, code interpreters, browsersYour servers on Docker or Kubernetes; gVisor, Kata or FirecrackerYes, Apache-2.0You run and scale the servers
E2B, DaytonaAgent code in hosted sandboxesThe vendor's cloud, with an open-source corePartlyPay as you go; code runs on someone else's machines
PotluckEach job in a fresh VM or sandboxSpare Macs (Tart) and Linux boxes (Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor) on your teamYes, Apache-2.0Early; the host machine can read what runs on it

The hosted services do well when you want no machines to look after. The self-hosted options do well when you already have hardware and want code to stay on it.

What the Claude Code sandbox restricts

Anthropic's Claude Code documentation describes the Bash sandbox as a boundary that the operating system enforces around shell commands. On macOS it uses Seatbelt, which ships with the system. On Linux and WSL2 it needs bubblewrap and socat from your package manager. On native Windows, commands run unsandboxed, so the docs point Windows users to WSL2.

With it on, by default:

  • Writes go only to the working directory, a per-user temp directory and directories you added. Claude Code's own settings, hooks directories and shell startup files stay write-protected.
  • Reads cover most of the machine, including ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials. You close that with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead or the sandbox.credentials block.
  • Network has no direct route out. Traffic goes through a local proxy that checks each hostname against allowedDomains, which starts empty. Tools that ignore proxy variables, such as plain ssh and most database drivers, cannot connect at all.
  • Environment variables are inherited, secrets included, unless you deny or mask them.

To turn it on, run /sandbox in a session and pick auto-allow or regular permissions. To turn it on everywhere, set sandbox.enabled to true in ~/.claude/settings.json. To check it works, ask Claude (not the ! prompt) to run touch ~/sandbox-probe; inside the sandbox it should fail.

What runs outside it

This is the part people miss. The Claude Code docs list what the Bash sandbox does not cover:

  • The built-in Read, Edit, Write, WebFetch and WebSearch tools, which follow permission rules instead.
  • Hooks, local MCP servers, LSP servers and helper commands, which run with your full access.
  • Commands you type yourself at the ! prompt, in most sessions.
  • Commands matched by excludedCommands, and commands Claude retries unsandboxed after a failure. Setting allowUnsandboxedCommands to false turns that retry off.

The docs also say plainly that the sandbox reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary, and that the proxy does not inspect TLS by default. Their advice for putting everything behind one boundary is to run the Claude Code process itself in a container, a VM or the sandbox runtime.

Some common tools also fail inside it: docker, jest with watchman, and on Linux, Chromium and rootless Podman. Each workaround gives up some isolation.

How to run Claude Code in a sandbox on your own computer

Pick by what you want to protect:

  1. Protect your files and network from stray shell commands. Turn on /sandbox, deny reads of credential paths, keep allowedDomains short, and turn off unsandboxed retries. This costs nothing and stays on your laptop.
  2. Protect your whole machine from the agent. Run Claude Code inside a dev container, a local VM or the sandbox runtime. Everything the agent starts is inside the boundary, but it shares your laptop's CPU and memory.
  3. Keep the agent's commands off your laptop entirely. Send the commands to a throwaway sandbox on another machine. This is where OpenSandbox, the hosted services and Potluck sit.

Many teams do 1 and 3 together: the built-in sandbox for local work, and a separate box for builds, tests and anything that needs network access you would not grant on your own machine.

Open-source, self-hosted sandboxes for AI coding agents

OpenSandbox manages the sandbox lifecycle (start, monitor, pause, terminate) on Docker for local testing and Kubernetes for production. It ships SDKs in several languages, lets you choose gVisor, Kata Containers or Firecracker for isolation, and has an MCP server so Claude Code or Cursor can call it. You run and scale the servers yourself.

Anthropic's sandbox runtime is the open-source package the Claude Code sandbox is built on. You can use it on its own to wrap the whole Claude Code process on one machine.

Potluck takes a different angle: it does not ship its own sandbox runtime. It drives Tart on Apple silicon Macs, and Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux (Incus is also supported), and it pools the idle machines a team already owns. Each job gets a fresh VM or sandbox. It runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account. It is not a hosted cloud and not a scheduler for clusters.

What Potluck does for agents today:

  • potluck --pool friends mcp runs an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent, so Claude Code can run commands in a pooled sandbox instead of on your laptop. More in give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP.
  • potluck agent-runner runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes.
  • On the OCI layer the default is no network at all, and potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

What to know before you use it:

  • The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, secrets included. The machine that runs a pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust.
  • A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
  • Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac (Potluck facts). Lending them to your team is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not. This is not legal advice.

See the agent sandbox page and run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines for more.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that will run the pool:

potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host

The first create prints a Tailscale login URL. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure. Ana runs potluck join '<code>' to use sandboxes. Carl first checks his spare box with potluck doctor and potluck host --dry-run, then runs potluck host '<code>'. That checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size, and joins only when a size passes. By default --share is 0.5, so half the cores and RAM are shared (Potluck facts). potluck host stop ends sharing.

A worked example from Ana's laptop:

potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>

To hand the pool to Claude Code, register potluck --pool friends mcp as an MCP server. For Mac specifics, see Tart; for spreading work over several boxes, see pool spare Macs and Linux boxes.

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

Questions people ask

Is the Claude Code sandbox on by default?

No. Anthropic's docs say it is off until you run /sandbox or set sandbox.enabled to true in a settings file.

Does the Claude Code sandbox cover file edits and MCP servers?

No. It covers shell commands and their child processes. The Read, Edit and Write tools, hooks and local MCP servers run outside it.

Anthropic's sandbox runtime for one machine, OpenSandbox on your own Docker or Kubernetes servers, and Potluck for pooling a team's spare Macs and Linux boxes. All are open source; you supply the hardware.

The Claude Code docs say native Windows runs commands unsandboxed and recommend WSL2. To share a machine in a Potluck pool you need an Apple silicon Mac or a Linux box.

entry.title: Open-Source Self-Hosted Coding Agents and CI on Your Own Machines (November 2026)
entry.summary: Which open-source tools run coding agents and CI jobs on machines you already own, as of November 2026: agents, runners, sandboxes and where Potluck fits.
entry.content:
Short answer: To run coding agents and CI jobs on machines you already own with open-source software, you need two pieces: an agent and a safe place to run it and your builds. For the agent, OpenHands and OpenCode are MIT-licensed according to their repositories, and Cline's CLI, Desktop and VS Code surfaces are Apache-2.0 according to its repository. For the machines, Potluck, free and Apache-2.0, made by Sengi, Inc., pools a team's idle Macs and Linux boxes and runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on them, each in a fresh VM or sandbox, with at most two macOS guests per Mac (Apple's licence). Potluck is early: a real Actions job has gone through it by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but it does not yet run daily in its makers' own CI.

Two jobs: the agent, and the machine it runs on

Most pages about self-hosted coding agents compare agents. That is half the question. The searches behind this post ask for something that runs agents and CI jobs on machines you already own, which splits into:

  • The agent or harness. The program that reads code, calls a model and runs commands. OpenHands, OpenCode, Cline, Coder Agents, or a CLI such as Claude Code or Codex.
  • The execution layer. The machine, VM or sandbox where those commands and your CI jobs actually run, and what that box can reach.

An agent on your laptop runs with your shell, your files and your network. A CI job on a self-hosted runner runs on whatever host you installed it on. Neither is isolated unless you add isolation. Potluck works on the second job: it turns spare Macs and Linux boxes into a pool that hands out fresh VMs and sandboxes, and it drives existing runtimes (Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus) instead of shipping its own.

Potluck is made by Sengi, which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project that runs without Sengi or a Sengi account. Licences below are as stated by each project's own repository or docs.

These combine. A team can run OpenCode or OpenHands as the agent and point its command execution at Potluck sandboxes, and keep GitHub's runner for some jobs while moving others to fresh VMs.

How Potluck plugs into agents and CI

Potluck exposes the pool in four ways.

Sandboxes from the command line. potluck sandbox create prints an id, potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a runs a command inside it, and potluck sandbox rm <id> removes it. Any script or agent that can run a shell command can use these. More in run coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines and on the agent sandbox page.

An MCP server for agents. potluck --pool friends mcp starts an MCP server that exposes sandbox tools to an agent, so an agent that speaks MCP can create a box, run commands in it and throw it away. See give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP.

Vendor agent runners. potluck agent-runner runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes, so a hosted agent product that supports self-hosted runners executes on your hardware instead of a long-lived host.

GitHub Actions. A runner broker sends Actions jobs to fresh VMs or sandboxes. As of today a real Actions job has been run through it, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine using OCI with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in our own CI, so treat it as something to try, not something to move your release pipeline onto. Details on the GitHub Actions runner page and in self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac.

What stays on your machines, and what still leaves

Self-hosting execution keeps the repository clone, build outputs and the credentials the job uses on hardware you own. It does not, by itself, keep everything local:

  • The model request. Where prompts and the file contents an agent reads are sent is set by the agent's own configuration. With a hosted model they go to that provider. OpenHands, OpenCode and Cline each document local model servers such as Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM if prompts must stay in your network.
  • The host can read the guest. In Potluck, the machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs a pool can read the commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and keep production secrets out of pools that include machines you do not control.
  • Network reach. Whatever a box can reach, an agent in it can reach. potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. On the OCI layer the default is no network at all, which also means a job that needs to download packages needs network you choose to give it.

There are no promises here: use it at your own risk, and verify the boundaries you care about on your own setup.

What each machine needs

  • Mac: Tart on an Apple silicon Mac. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice. See the Tart page.
  • Linux: Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor.
  • Sharing: --share sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, and Potluck's default is 0.5, half the machine.
  • Taking a machine back: a Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.

Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure. For a longer walkthrough of a mixed pool, see pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that runs the pool:

potluck create friends
potluck invite ana
potluck invite carl --host

The first potluck create prints a Tailscale login URL. potluck invite ana makes a code for a friend who runs sandboxes; potluck invite carl --host makes a code for a friend who shares a machine.

A friend who wants sandboxes runs potluck join '<code>'. A friend sharing a machine first runs potluck doctor to see what it can share and potluck host --dry-run to print the plan, then potluck host '<code>'. That checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. potluck host stop stops sharing.

Then try a box:

potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it and say what breaks: a machine that fails the conformance check, a runner job that hangs, an agent that cannot reach its sandbox. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions with what you ran and what happened. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues. The source is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.

Questions people ask

What open-source tools run coding agents and CI jobs on machines I already own?

For the agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Cline's open-source surfaces and Coder Agents all run on your own hardware. For execution, GitHub's self-hosted runner runs Actions jobs on a host you own, and Potluck runs Actions jobs and coding agents in fresh VMs or sandboxes across a pool of your Macs and Linux boxes.

Is Potluck a coding agent?

No. Potluck gives agents and CI jobs a place to run: fresh sandboxes from the command line, an MCP server with sandbox tools, and potluck agent-runner for a vendor's self-hosted runners. You bring the agent.

Can I run an open-source coding agent fully locally?

The agent and its commands can run entirely on your machines. The model request leaves unless you point the agent at a local model server, which OpenHands, OpenCode and Cline each document; check the agent's telemetry and update settings too.

Does Potluck run GitHub Actions jobs today?

A real Actions job has been run through its runner broker by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box with OCI and gVisor. It is not yet running daily in its makers' own CI, so it is ready to try, not to depend on.

What does Potluck cost?

Potluck is free and open source under Apache-2.0, and it runs without Sengi or a Sengi account. Your cost is the machines you already own.

Can I lend my Mac to friends for builds?

Yes, to your team or invited friends, with at most two macOS guests per Mac as Apple's licence allows. Selling Mac time to the public or pooling iOS Simulator time is not allowed; this is not legal advice.

Is my code safe on someone else's machine?

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, and the pool's machine can read commands and output. Join only pools whose owner you trust, and keep secrets you cannot afford to expose out of shared pools.

Do I need Kubernetes?

No. Potluck is not a cluster scheduler; it runs on individual Macs and Linux boxes with Tart, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor.

entry.title: Claude Code Docker sandbox and devcontainer setup (2026)
entry.summary: Four ways to run Claude Code in a sandbox in 2026: built-in sandbox, devcontainer, Docker Sandboxes, your own image, plus spare team machines.
entry.content:
Short answer: As of November 2026 there are four common ways to run Claude Code locally in a sandbox. The first is its built-in sandbox, turned on with the /sandbox command or the sandbox block in .claude/settings.local.json, which uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux. The second is Anthropic's reference devcontainer, a Docker container plus a firewall. The third is Docker Sandboxes, where sbx run claude ~/my-project starts one microVM per sandbox. The fourth is your own Docker image run as a non-root user. The Claude Code material these searches lead to describes no claude sandbox subcommand. The Claude Code program runs on your machine, but the default models run at Anthropic, so you need an API key or a Claude subscription. Anthropic says its sandbox cuts permission prompts by 84%, as quoted in a write-up by the consultancy Sourcelabs. If you want the commands to run on a spare Mac or Linux box instead of your laptop, Potluck is a different route. It is free, open source and early, and it gives an agent fresh sandboxes on machines your team already owns, with at most two macOS guests per Mac.

The options compared

OptionHow you start itIsolation boundaryNetwork controlWhere it costs more or needs more work
Claude Code built-in sandbox/sandbox in a session, or sandbox in settingsOS level: Seatbelt (macOS), bubblewrap (Linux)Allow lists in settingsThe sandboxed shell skips your profile, so tools may be missing from PATH. Settings live on each machine
Anthropic reference devcontainerReopen the repo in the container from your editorDocker container plus a firewall scriptFirewall limits outbound hostsNeeds Docker and an editor that understands devcontainers. You maintain the image
Docker Sandboxes (sbx)sbx run claude ~/my-projectmicroVM with its own Docker daemon, filesystem and networkPolicy presets such as Balanced and Locked DownNeeds the sbx CLI and a Docker sign-in. Does not read your ~/.claude
Your own Docker imagedocker run, then docker execContainerWhatever you configureYou handle credentials, the non-root user, caches and cleanup
Potluckpotluck sandbox create, or potluck --pool friends mcpFresh VM (Tart on a Mac) or sandbox (Kata or gVisor on Linux) on a team machineNo network at all by default on the OCI layerEarly. Needs a spare machine and Tailscale or a tunnel. The host machine can read what runs in it

Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which also sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project and needs no Sengi account.

Is there a claude sandbox command?

People search for claude sandbox, claude --sandbox and claude sandbox run. The Claude Code material these searches lead to describes switching sandboxing on in two ways: the /sandbox command inside an interactive session, or the sandbox block in a settings file. It does not describe a separate claude sandbox subcommand.

The command that does start Claude Code in a sandbox from one line is Docker's: sbx run claude. That is the Docker Sandboxes CLI, not Claude Code.

Claude Code's built-in sandbox and settings.local.json

Claude Code reads settings from three places:

  • ~/.claude/settings.json is your user file and applies to every project.
  • .claude/settings.json is the project file you commit.
  • .claude/settings.local.json is a project file you keep out of git, which suits per-machine sandbox paths.

The smallest useful local file turns the sandbox on:

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true
  }
}

The filesystem and network rules people search for as sandbox.filesystem and sandbox.network go inside that same sandbox block. In them you list extra write paths, such as build caches like ~/.m2 and ~/.npm, and the hosts the shell may reach, such as your package registry. Key names have shifted between Claude Code releases, so copy them from the settings reference that matches your installed version rather than from an old blog post.

Two lessons from the Sourcelabs write-up, whose authors ran Claude Code headless in a pipeline:

  • PATH. Inside the Seatbelt sandbox the shell did not load .zshrc or .bashrc, so node and mvn were not found. They had to resolve tool paths on the host and pass them in.
  • Headless settings. In their setup, project-level sandbox settings did not apply to claude -p runs, so they fell back to the user file in ~/.claude.

The built-in sandbox works well for interactive sessions on your own laptop, where you can answer a prompt when a rule blocks something. For unattended runs it needs more setup up front.

Anthropic's reference devcontainer

Anthropic publishes a reference devcontainer that runs Claude Code inside a Docker container, with a firewall layer limiting where it can connect. You open the repository in an editor that supports devcontainers and reopen it in the container. Claude Code then runs inside, against your mounted project.

This is the setup Anthropic points to when you want --dangerously-skip-permissions: the container is the boundary, so skipping prompts is less risky.

The cost is that you own the image. Your toolchain, caches and credentials all have to be set up in it. The Sourcelabs team chose to disable Claude Code's own sandbox inside their container, with { "sandbox": { "enabled": false } }, because Seatbelt and bubblewrap rules can clash with a containerised environment. Anthropic's reference keeps it on and adds the firewall.

Docker Sandboxes: sbx run claude

Docker Sandboxes is the shortest path from nothing to Claude Code in an isolated box, according to Docker's documentation:

  1. Install the sbx CLI and sign in to Docker.
  2. Store an API key with sbx secret set anthropic, or skip it and use /login inside Claude Code for a subscription.
  3. Run sbx run --name my-sandbox claude from your project directory. On the first run, pick a network preset. Balanced allows common development services and asks about the rest.
  4. Check status with sbx ls, stop with sbx stop my-sandbox, and remove with sbx rm my-sandbox.

What Docker's docs say it does:

  • Each sandbox is a microVM with its own Docker daemon. The agent can build images and start containers without touching your host.
  • The default start command is claude --dangerously-skip-permissions.
  • Your project directory is mounted read-write. --clone gives the agent a private clone instead, which helps when several agents work on one repository.
  • Hosts can be allowed one by one with sbx policy allow network.

One catch: the sandbox does not pick up user-level configuration such as ~/.claude, only project-level files in the working directory.

Your own Docker image

If you run Claude Code in a pipeline, a plain image is easy to reason about. This one follows the Sourcelabs example:

FROM node:22-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git jq
RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
RUN useradd -m -s /bin/bash claude
USER claude

The non-root user matters. Sourcelabs found that Claude Code refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions when run as root.

They also changed how they used containers. At first every step started a fresh container, which re-downloaded dependencies each time. They switched to one named container per ticket and ran each step in it with docker exec.

You also have to get credentials in. That means an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable, or the OAuth credentials file on Linux.

Running the sandbox on another machine with Potluck

Every option above runs on the machine in front of you. Potluck asks a different question: what if the commands Claude Code runs happen on a spare Mac mini or Linux box in the office, in a fresh VM or sandbox each time, while Claude Code stays on your laptop?

Potluck exposes sandbox tools to an agent over MCP with potluck --pool friends mcp. You register that command as an MCP server in Claude Code. The agent can then create a sandbox, run commands in it and remove it, on whichever pool machine has room. There is more on this in give your AI agent a sandbox over MCP.

On the Linux OCI layer the default is no network at all. That suits running untrusted build and test commands, but it means you would not run Claude Code itself inside such a box by default, since it has to reach Anthropic. Keep Claude Code where your credentials already are and send the commands out.

Also keep the trust model in mind. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. The machine that runs the pool can read commands and output passing through it.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed), then start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

Create a pool and invite people. On the machine that runs the pool, run potluck create friends. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL. Then:

  • potluck invite ana makes a code for someone who will run sandboxes.
  • potluck invite carl --host makes a code for someone who will share a machine.

They run potluck join '<code>' or potluck host '<code>'.

Share a machine. Sharing needs Tart on an Apple silicon Mac, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. Check first with potluck doctor and potluck host --dry-run. --share sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared; the default is 0.5, per the Potluck docs. potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet. potluck host stop stops sharing.

Try a sandbox by hand:

potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>

See the agent sandbox page and running coding agents in a sandbox on your own machines for longer walkthroughs.

What makes Potluck different

  • It uses machines you already own. Claude Code's commands run on the Macs and Linux boxes your team already has, not on your laptop and not on rented machines.
  • A borrowed Mac goes back to its owner. A Mac sandbox ends the moment its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.
  • One pool for agents and CI. The same pool serves coding-agent sandboxes and GitHub Actions jobs, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. A real Actions job has been run through it by hand on a Mac and on Linux, but it is not yet in daily use in Potluck's own CI.
  • Agents get sandbox tools over MCP. Claude Code calls sandbox tools directly instead of shelling into your host.
  • Free and open source. Potluck is Apache-2.0 and runs without a Sengi account. Teammates and invited friends can lend machines to the same pool.

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to try it with Claude Code and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions. If you want to contribute, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

Questions people ask

Can I run Claude Code fully locally?

The Claude Code program runs locally, but with the default Anthropic models the model runs at Anthropic and needs an API key or a Claude subscription. Docker's documentation covers pointing Claude Code at local or hosted models instead.

How do I turn on the Claude Code sandbox?

Type /sandbox in an interactive session, or set "sandbox": { "enabled": true } in .claude/settings.local.json or another settings file. It uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux.

Should I use the devcontainer or Docker Sandboxes?

The devcontainer gives you a container you fully control and can commit to the repo. Docker Sandboxes gives you a microVM with its own Docker daemon and network policy from one command, but needs the sbx CLI and a Docker sign-in.

Why does Claude Code fail as root in Docker?

Claude Code refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions when run as root, as the Sourcelabs write-up reports. Create a non-root user in your Dockerfile and switch to it.

Can Potluck run Claude Code's commands on a spare Mac?

Potluck gives Claude Code sandbox tools over MCP, so its commands run in fresh VMs on a spare Mac (Tart, Apple silicon) or Linux box. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac.

Is a Potluck sandbox safe for my API key?

The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, so only put keys on machines whose owners you trust. Potluck makes no promises; use it at your own risk.

entry.title: Self-Hosted GitHub Actions Runner Alternatives to Blacksmith and Cirrus Runners (November 2026)
entry.summary: Self-hosted alternatives to Blacksmith and Cirrus Runners, November 2026: GitHub's runner app, ARC, Tart and Potluck on machines you own.
entry.content:
Short answer: if you already own Macs or Linux boxes, the alternatives to Blacksmith and Cirrus Runners are GitHub's own self-hosted runner, Actions Runner Controller on a Kubernetes cluster, or a pool such as Potluck that runs each job in a fresh VM or sandbox on machines your team owns. GitHub's billing documentation describes self-hosted runner usage as free of a per-minute charge as of autumn 2026, so on your own hardware you pay for the machines, the power and your time rather than a rate per minute. Blacksmith and Cirrus Runners are managed services: you pay them for machines they run, and in return you do no hardware work. Potluck is free and open source, made by Sengi, Inc., which also sells hosted GitHub Actions runners, so weigh our view with that in mind. Potluck is early: a real Actions job has run through it by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but it does not yet run our own CI every day.

The options side by side

This table compares the options for someone deciding between paying for hosted runners and using hardware they already have. Prices change often, so check each vendor's pricing page on the day you decide; we only describe how each one bills.

OptionWho runs the hardwareHow you paymacOS jobsLinux jobsFresh machine per jobWork for you
GitHub-hosted runnersGitHubPer minute after plan allowanceYesYesYesNone
BlacksmithBlacksmithPer minute, with a free monthly allowanceYes, Apple siliconYes, x64 and ARMYes, microVMsInstall an app, change the label
Cirrus RunnersCirrus LabsFlat fee per runner per monthYes, Apple siliconCheck their siteYesInstall an app, change the label
GitHub self-hosted runner appYouYour machines and timeYesYesOnly if you build itPatching, cleanup, isolation
Actions Runner ControllerYou, on KubernetesYour cluster and timeNo, Linux containersYesYes, ephemeral podsRun and upgrade a cluster
Potluck (early)You and your teamFree; your machinesYes, via TartYes, via Kata or gVisorYes, VM or sandbox per jobInstall, host, join a pool

Blacksmith: what it does well and what it costs you

Blacksmith is a managed runner service for GitHub Actions focused on speed and price. You install its GitHub App and change runs-on to a Blacksmith label. Jobs run in microVMs on Linux x64 and ARM, with macOS on Apple silicon and Windows not yet generally available, and it adds a colocated cache, Docker layer caching on persistent disks, and SSH into running jobs. It bills per minute with a free monthly allowance.

It costs more than self-hosting when you already own idle machines, because you pay for every minute on hardware someone else runs. It costs less in your time: there is nothing to patch and no box under a desk to reboot.

Cirrus Runners and Cirrus CI: which is which

Cirrus Labs has made several products, and the names get mixed up in searches:

  • Cirrus CI is a full CI service with its own configuration file, separate from GitHub Actions.
  • Cirrus Runners are managed Apple silicon machines that plug into GitHub Actions as runners. They are billed as a flat monthly fee per runner instead of per minute, which suits teams with steady macOS load.
  • Tart is Cirrus Labs' open-source tool for running macOS and Linux VMs on Apple silicon. Potluck drives Tart on Macs; see Tart.

Cirrus Labs has announced changes to Cirrus CI over time, so check their site for what is offered today before you plan around either product. If the reason you looked at Cirrus Runners was "fresh macOS VMs for Actions jobs", the self-hosted version of that is Tart on a Mac you own, which is what Potluck sets up for you.

What self-hosting costs per minute in 2026

The search "GitHub self-hosted runner pricing per minute 2026" has a short answer and a caveat.

  • GitHub's charge: GitHub's billing documentation describes self-hosted runner usage as free. GitHub did announce a per-minute platform charge for self-hosted usage in private repositories and then postponed it to re-evaluate. It has not been cancelled, so check GitHub's billing page and budget for it returning in some form.
  • Your hardware: a Mac or Linux box you already own and leave idle overnight costs you power, not a new purchase.
  • Your time: this is the real cost. GitHub's runner app does not give you a clean VM per job; leftover files, caches and processes carry from one job to the next unless you build cleanup. GitHub also warns against self-hosted runners on public repositories, because a pull request from a stranger runs on your machine.

Potluck's aim is to cut the time cost: each job gets a fresh VM or sandbox, and the machine joins a pool only after it passes a conformance check.

Can you run GitHub Actions on spare Macs instead of hosted macOS runners?

Yes. macOS minutes are the most expensive kind on hosted services, and a spare Apple silicon Mac is often sitting idle. There are three ways to do it:

  1. GitHub's runner app directly on the Mac. Fastest to set up, no isolation between jobs. We walk through it in a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on your Mac.
  2. Tart VMs you script yourself. Each job gets a fresh macOS VM; you write the glue that starts the VM, registers the runner and deletes it.
  3. Potluck. It drives Tart for you and hands each job a fresh VM. A real Actions job has been run through Potluck's runner broker by hand on a Mac with Tart, and on a Linux box on another machine with gVisor. It is not yet running in our own CI every day, so treat it as early. See GitHub Actions runner for the current state.

Two limits apply to any Mac option:

  • Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.
  • Owners come first. In Potluck, a Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. A build on a Mac someone is using will be cut off, so pool Macs that sit idle, such as an old Mac mini or a laptop overnight.

What Potluck is and is not

Potluck puts a team's idle Macs and Linux boxes to work, running GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on machines you already own, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. It is not a hosted cloud, it is not a sandbox runtime of its own (it drives Tart, Kata, gVisor and Incus), and it is not a cluster scheduler. It runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

To share a machine you need Tart on an Apple silicon Mac, or Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor on Linux. Machines reach each other over Tailscale, or over a tunnel you configure. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. Hand-back when the owner returns works on a Mac; on Linux it works only as a time window today.

Trust matters here. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets passed to a build. The machine that runs the pool can read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust, and use it at your own risk. For more on pooling, read pool spare Macs and Linux boxes for builds and agents.

Which option fits

  • No spare hardware, want zero upkeep: GitHub-hosted runners or Blacksmith.
  • Steady macOS load, want a fixed monthly bill: a flat-fee managed Mac service such as Cirrus Runners, if it is offered when you read this.
  • A Kubernetes cluster already running, Linux jobs only: Actions Runner Controller.
  • One spare Mac, a private repository, and you accept shared state between jobs: GitHub's runner app on the Mac.
  • Several idle Macs and Linux boxes across a team, want a fresh VM per job, willing to try early software: Potluck.

You can mix them. The runner is chosen per job by the runs-on label, so Linux jobs can stay on a hosted service while macOS jobs move to a Mac you own.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that will run the pool, create it. The first time, it prints a Tailscale login URL. Then make an invite code for a friend who will share a machine:

potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host

On the spare Mac or Linux box, check what it can share, look at the plan, then host:

potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'

potluck host checks the machine, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size and joins the pool only when a size passes. --share sets the fraction of cores and RAM shared, 0.5 by default. potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet; on the OCI layer the default is no network at all. potluck host stop stops sharing.

To try a sandbox by hand:

potluck sandbox create
potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a
potluck sandbox rm <id>

For coding agents, potluck --pool friends mcp exposes sandbox tools over MCP, and potluck agent-runner runs a coding-agent vendor's self-hosted runners in fresh sandboxes. See agent sandbox.

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to install it, host a machine, run a job and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions with your hardware and what happened. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

Questions people ask

What are the alternatives to Cirrus Runners and Blacksmith if I have my own hardware?

GitHub's self-hosted runner app, Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes, scripted Tart VMs on Macs, or Potluck, which runs each job in a fresh VM or sandbox on machines your team owns. All of them use hardware you already pay for instead of a per-minute or per-runner fee.

Does GitHub charge per minute for self-hosted runners in 2026?

GitHub's billing documentation describes self-hosted runner usage as free of a per-minute charge as of autumn 2026. GitHub announced a platform charge for self-hosted usage and postponed it, so check its billing page before you budget.

What is the difference between Cirrus CI and Cirrus Runners?

Cirrus CI is a separate CI service with its own configuration, while Cirrus Runners are managed Apple silicon machines that run GitHub Actions jobs for a flat monthly fee per runner. Cirrus Labs also makes Tart, the VM tool Potluck uses on Macs.

How many macOS VMs can I run on one Mac?

Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac. Lending them to your team is fine; selling Mac time to the public is not. This is not legal advice.

Can Potluck replace Blacksmith for my whole CI today?

Not yet. A real Actions job has run through Potluck by hand on a Mac and on a Linux box, but it is not yet running in our own CI every day, so start with a few jobs, not your main pipeline.

Is it safe to run builds on a teammate's machine?

Only if you trust them. The machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets, and the pool's machine can read commands and output, so join only pools whose owner you trust.

What happens if the Mac's owner sits down during a build?

The Mac sandbox ends as soon as the owner touches the keyboard or pointer, and the job fails. Pool Macs that are idle for long stretches.

entry.title: The best way to get self-hosted macOS runners with a fresh VM for every job (November 2026)
entry.summary: Self-hosted macOS runners with a fresh VM per job, November 2026: hosted runners, Tart and Cilicon, or Potluck, and the two-VM-per-Mac limit.
entry.content:
Short answer: The best way to get self-hosted macOS runners with a fresh VM for every job is to run each job in a throwaway Tart VM on an Apple silicon Mac, cloned from a runner image and deleted after that one job. The number to plan around is two: Apple's macOS licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, so each Mac runs at most two fresh-VM jobs at once, and four parallel macOS jobs need two Macs. You can get there with a hosted macOS runner service, with Tart and Cilicon on a Mac you own or rent, or with Potluck, a free, early, Apache-2.0 project that pools the Macs your team already owns and caps macOS guests at two per Mac. If you are leaving Cirrus Runners, its macOS runner images are public OCI images, so any Tart-based path keeps the same build environment.

Disclosure: Potluck is made by Sengi, Inc., which sells hosted GitHub Actions runners. Potluck is a separate free project. This post compares both kinds of option.

The options compared

OptionWhere jobs runFresh VM per jobSetup workCost shapeStatus
GitHub-hosted macOS runnersGitHub's MacsYesNonePer-minute billingMature
Other hosted runner services (Sengi is one)The provider's MacsDepends on providerLowPer minute or per monthVaries
Rented dedicated Mac with Tart and CiliconA Mac you rent, for example from OakHostYes, Cilicon cycles VMsGitHub App, config file, auto-loginMonthly rentTools in public use
Your own Mac with Tart and CiliconHardware you ownYesSame as above, plus hardware careHardware you already paid forTools in public use
Potluck on Macs your team ownsSpare Macs and Linux boxes in a poolYes, fresh Tart VM or sandboxInstall script, create pool, hostFree, Apache-2.0Early; Actions jobs run by hand so far

No prices are shown because they change. Check each provider's own page.

Why people are looking for this now

OakHost, a Mac hosting company, published a migration guide this year. It reports that Cirrus Labs is joining OpenAI's Agent Infrastructure group, that Cirrus CI is shutting down, and that Cirrus Runners no longer accepts new customers. Cirrus Runners gave teams what this search asks for: each GitHub Actions job ran in a fresh macOS VM built with Tart, the VM tool Cirrus Labs wrote. Teams that relied on it now have to rebuild that setup somewhere else, and most want to keep the one-job-per-VM model.

Why a fresh VM per job matters

A long-lived macOS runner collects state. Homebrew packages, simulator runtimes, keychain entries, DerivedData and environment changes stay behind, so a build can pass only because of something an earlier job left. A fresh VM per job removes that:

  • Clean start: every job boots from the same image, so a green build means the image and your code are enough.
  • No leftover secrets: tokens and signing material from one job are gone before the next job starts.
  • Easy rollback: a bad image change is fixed by pointing back at the previous image tag.

The cost is boot time and disk space. Plan room for at least one full image on each Mac.

Option 1: hosted macOS runners

GitHub's own macOS runners give each job a new VM with no setup. They are the simplest choice if GitHub's images suit you and the per-minute bill fits. Other hosted services, including Sengi, run Macs for you and differ in image choice, concurrency and billing. Hosted runners do well on zero maintenance, no hardware and no licence counting on your side. They cost more as your minutes grow, and you depend on the provider staying in business, which is what the Cirrus Runners shutdown shows.

Option 2: Tart and Cilicon on a Mac you own or rent

This is the path OakHost's guide describes, and it is closest to what Cirrus Runners did. Tart creates and runs macOS VMs on Apple silicon using Apple's Virtualization framework, and its images are OCI images. Cilicon is a macOS app on top of Tart: it clones the image, boots the VM, registers an ephemeral GitHub Actions runner inside it, waits for one job, destroys the VM and repeats.

The work, in outline:

  1. Get an Apple silicon Mac, your own or a rented dedicated one.
  2. Create a GitHub App for your organisation with read and write access to self-hosted runners, download its private key, and install the app.
  3. Write a Cilicon config that points at your runner image. Cirrus users can point at the same public macos-runner image tag.
  4. Start Cilicon, turn on automatic login and add Cilicon to login items so it survives a reboot.
  5. Change runs-on in your workflows from the Cirrus image reference to your self-hosted labels.

This works well on a dedicated machine and keeps your images unchanged. You patch the Mac, watch disk space and handle the GUI login requirement, and each Mac still tops out at two VMs. For the runner side, see self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on your Mac and our Tart page.

Option 3: Potluck on the Macs your team already owns

Many teams have Apple silicon Macs that sit idle much of the day: an old Mac mini, a spare laptop, a build box nobody watches. Potluck puts those machines in a pool and runs GitHub Actions jobs and coding agents on them, each in a fresh VM or sandbox. On a Mac it uses Tart. On Linux it uses Docker or Podman with Kata or gVisor, so Linux jobs can go to Linux boxes in the same pool. It runs without Sengi and without a Sengi account.

What is true today, from the Potluck project facts:

  • A real GitHub Actions job has been run through Potluck's runner broker, by hand, on a Mac with Tart and on a Linux box on another machine with gVisor. It is not yet running daily in the project's own CI.
  • When a machine joins as a host, Potluck checks it, pulls the image, runs a quick conformance check per size, and joins the pool only when a size passes.
  • --share sets the fraction of cores and RAM a host gives the pool; the default is 0.5.
  • Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac, matching Apple's licence.
  • A Mac sandbox ends when its owner touches the keyboard or pointer. When an owner takes a machine back, running VMs end and new work is refused. On Linux, hand-back works only as a time window today.

That last point decides where Potluck fits. On a Mac someone is using, a job can be cut short when they sit down, so use Macs nobody sits at for CI, or expect reruns. See the GitHub Actions runner page and pooling spare Macs and Linux boxes.

What to check before you move jobs

  • Concurrency: divide your peak number of parallel macOS jobs by two to get the number of Macs you need on any self-hosted path.
  • Images: keep your current image tag at first, and change images separately from changing where jobs run.
  • Trust: the machine that runs a VM can read everything in it, including secrets. With Potluck, the machine that runs the pool can also read commands and output passing through it. Join only a pool whose owner you trust.
  • Licence: lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine. Selling Mac time to the public is not, and neither is pooling iOS Simulator time. This is not legal advice.
  • Network: decide what a job may reach. potluck isolation test <size> checks that a box cannot reach the host, its LAN or its tailnet.

How to start with Potluck

Install on macOS or Linux (no Go needed) and start the daemon:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sengirunners/potluck/main/install.sh | sh
potluck daemon --detach

On the machine that will run the pool:

potluck create friends
potluck invite carl --host

The first create prints a Tailscale login URL. Machines reach each other over Tailscale or over a tunnel you configure. On each spare Mac, check it and then share it:

potluck doctor
potluck host --dry-run
potluck host '<code>'

Run potluck isolation test <size> to confirm isolation, and potluck host stop to stop sharing. To try a sandbox by hand: potluck sandbox create, then potluck sandbox exec <id> -- uname -a, then potluck sandbox rm <id>. Sharing a Mac needs Tart on Apple silicon. The code is at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck.

Try it early

Potluck is early. Its makers want people with a spare Mac or Linux box to install it, run a job or a sandbox, and say what breaks. Start a thread at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/discussions with what you tried and what happened. If you want to contribute code, the good first issues are at https://github.com/sengirunners/potluck/issues.

Questions people ask

How many fresh macOS VMs can one Mac run at once?

Two. Apple's licence allows up to two macOS VMs on a Mac you own, and Potluck caps macOS guests at two per Mac for that reason.

Can I keep using my Cirrus Runners images?

Yes, on any Tart-based path. OakHost's migration guide notes that the Cirrus macOS runner images are public OCI images, so Tart can pull the same tag you used before.

Is Potluck ready to replace my Mac CI today?

Not yet for critical pipelines. A real Actions job has run through its runner broker by hand on a Mac and on Linux, but it is not yet running daily in the project's own CI, so try it on a workflow you can afford to rerun.

Do I need a Sengi account to use Potluck?

No. Potluck is free, Apache-2.0 licensed, and runs without Sengi or a Sengi account. Sengi sells hosted runners as a separate business.

Can I pool iOS Simulator time or rent my spare Macs to the public?

No. Lending a macOS guest to your team or invited friends is fine, but selling Mac time to the public and pooling iOS Simulator time are not. This is not legal advice.

Who can see my secrets on a self-hosted runner?

The machine that runs the VM can read everything in it, including secrets. In a Potluck pool, the machine that runs the pool can also read commands and output passing through it, so join only pools whose owner you trust.

entry.title: Tartelet vs Cilicon: ephemeral macOS GitHub Actions runners on Tart, autoscaling and Kubernetes (November 2026)
